Abstract Algebra — 00 · Integers, Relations and Modular Arithmetic

Created2026-07-04|Updated2026-07-04|Mathematics > Abstract Algebra
|Post View:

Abstract algebra studies structures: a set together with one or more operations that obey a short list of rules. Instead of asking "what is 7⋅137 \cdot 137⋅13?", it asks "which facts about multiplication follow from the rules alone, so that they hold for integers, for clock arithmetic, for matrices, for symmetries of a molecule, all at once?". That shift pays off in many places: symmetry (crystallography, chemistry, physics), cryptography (RSA and elliptic-curve systems are group theory in disguise), coding theory (error-correcting codes on every phone and disk are built over finite fields), and the classical question of solving polynomial equations, which Galois settled with groups. This series follows the standard senior undergraduate path of Dummit & Foote, Gallian, Artin and Fraleigh: groups, then rings and fields, then Galois theory. Post 00 lays the ground: the proof methods used throughout, sets and functions, equivalence relations, and the arithmetic of the integers up to modular arithmetic, the Chinese remainder theorem and a small but complete RSA example. Every later post uses Z\mathbb{Z}Z and Z/nZ\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}Z/nZ as its first examples.

Series map: 00 Integers, Relations & Modular Arithmetic (this post) → 01 Groups & Subgroups → 02 Cosets, Lagrange & Quotient Groups → 03 Homomorphisms, Group Actions & Sylow → 04 Rings, Ideals & Fields → 05 Field Extensions & Galois Theory.

Learning Outcome

  • Read and write the four basic proof patterns: direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction.
  • Decide whether a function is injective, surjective or bijective, and use the fact that bijections are exactly the invertible functions.
  • Prove that an equivalence relation on a set is the same thing as a partition of that set.
  • State and prove the division algorithm from the well-ordering principle.
  • Run the Euclidean algorithm and the extended Euclidean algorithm by hand, and prove Bézout's identity and Euclid's lemma.
  • Prove the fundamental theorem of arithmetic (existence and uniqueness).
  • Compute in Z/nZ\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}Z/nZ, find inverses, and decide which classes are units.
  • Use Euler's φ\varphiφ function, Fermat's little theorem and Euler's theorem to reduce huge powers.
  • Solve simultaneous congruences with the Chinese remainder theorem.
  • Carry out a toy RSA key generation, encryption and decryption, and explain why decryption works.

Chapter 1 — The proof toolkit

Abstract algebra is a proof-based subject. Almost every statement is an implication "if PPP then QQQ", and there are four standard ways to prove one.

Terminology

  • Proposition / theorem / lemma / corollary — a proved statement; a lemma is a helper, a corollary follows quickly from a theorem.
  • Definition — fixes the meaning of a word. Definitions are "if and only if" even when written with "if".
  • Contrapositive of "P⇒QP \Rightarrow QP⇒Q" is "not Q⇒Q \RightarrowQ⇒ not PPP". It is logically equivalent to the original.
  • Converse of "P⇒QP \Rightarrow QP⇒Q" is "Q⇒PQ \Rightarrow PQ⇒P". It is a different statement and may be false.
  • Counterexample — one concrete case that shows a universal statement is false.

Direct proof

Assume PPP, reason forward, reach QQQ.

Claim. The sum of two odd integers is even.

Proof. Odd integers can be written 2a+12a+12a+1 and 2b+12b+12b+1 with a,b∈Za, b \in \mathbb{Z}a,b∈Z. Their sum is 2a+2b+2=2(a+b+1)2a + 2b + 2 = 2(a+b+1)2a+2b+2=2(a+b+1), which is even. ■\blacksquare■

Proof by contrapositive

Prove "not Q⇒Q \RightarrowQ⇒ not PPP" instead.

Claim. If n2n^2n2 is even, then nnn is even.

Proof. Contrapositive: if nnn is odd then n2n^2n2 is odd. Write n=2k+1n = 2k+1n=2k+1; then n2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2+2k) + 1n2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1, which is odd. ■\blacksquare■

Proof by contradiction

Assume the statement is false and derive something impossible.

Claim. 2\sqrt{2}2​ is irrational.

Proof. Suppose 2=p/q\sqrt{2} = p/q2​=p/q with integers p,qp, qp,q, q≠0q \neq 0q=0, and the fraction in lowest terms. Then p2=2q2p^2 = 2q^2p2=2q2, so p2p^2p2 is even, so ppp is even by the previous claim. Write p=2mp = 2mp=2m: then 4m2=2q24m^2 = 2q^24m2=2q2, so q2=2m2q^2 = 2m^2q2=2m2 is even and qqq is even. Both ppp and qqq are even, contradicting lowest terms. ■\blacksquare■

Proof by induction

To prove a statement S(n)S(n)S(n) for all integers n≥n0n \geq n_0n≥n0​: prove S(n0)S(n_0)S(n0​) (the base case), then prove S(k)⇒S(k+1)S(k) \Rightarrow S(k+1)S(k)⇒S(k+1) for every k≥n0k \geq n_0k≥n0​ (the inductive step). In strong induction the inductive step may assume S(n0),…,S(k)S(n_0), \dots, S(k)S(n0​),…,S(k) all at once.

Claim. For every n≥1n \geq 1n≥1, 1+3+5+⋯+(2n−1)=n21 + 3 + 5 + \dots + (2n-1) = n^21+3+5+⋯+(2n−1)=n2.

Proof. Base case n=1n=1n=1: 1=121 = 1^21=12. Inductive step: if the sum of the first kkk odd numbers is k2k^2k2, adding the next one gives k2+(2k+1)=(k+1)2k^2 + (2k+1) = (k+1)^2k2+(2k+1)=(k+1)2. ■\blacksquare■

Watch out: proving the converse is not proving the statement. "If nnn is even then n2n^2n2 is even" is true, but it does not prove "if n2n^2n2 is even then nnn is even"; that needed its own proof above.

Chapter 2 — Sets, functions and equivalence relations

Terminology

  • N={0,1,2,… }\mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}N={0,1,2,…} (some books start at 1; this series includes 0), Z\mathbb{Z}Z the integers, Q\mathbb{Q}Q the rationals, R\mathbb{R}R the reals, C\mathbb{C}C the complex numbers.
  • A×B={(a,b):a∈A,b∈B}A \times B = \{(a, b) : a \in A, b \in B\}A×B={(a,b):a∈A,b∈B} is the Cartesian product.
  • A function f:A→Bf : A \to Bf:A→B assigns to each a∈Aa \in Aa∈A exactly one f(a)∈Bf(a) \in Bf(a)∈B. AAA is the domain, BBB the codomain, f(A)f(A)f(A) the image.
  • fff is injective (one-to-one) if f(a1)=f(a2)f(a_1) = f(a_2)f(a1​)=f(a2​) implies a1=a2a_1 = a_2a1​=a2​.
  • fff is surjective (onto) if every b∈Bb \in Bb∈B equals f(a)f(a)f(a) for some aaa.
  • fff is bijective if it is both. A bijection from a set to itself is a permutation of the set.
  • A relation on AAA is a subset R⊆A×AR \subseteq A \times AR⊆A×A; write a∼ba \sim ba∼b when (a,b)∈R(a, b) \in R(a,b)∈R.

Functions and inverses

Examples on Z\mathbb{Z}Z: f(x)=2xf(x) = 2xf(x)=2x is injective but not surjective (odd numbers are missed). g(x)=⌊x/2⌋g(x) = \lfloor x/2 \rfloorg(x)=⌊x/2⌋ is surjective but not injective (g(0)=g(1)=0g(0) = g(1) = 0g(0)=g(1)=0). h(x)=x+5h(x) = x + 5h(x)=x+5 is bijective with inverse x↦x−5x \mapsto x - 5x↦x−5.

Proposition 2.1. A function f:A→Bf : A \to Bf:A→B has an inverse function g:B→Ag : B \to Ag:B→A (with g∘f=idAg \circ f = \mathrm{id}_Ag∘f=idA​ and f∘g=idBf \circ g = \mathrm{id}_Bf∘g=idB​) if and only if fff is bijective.

Proof. If ggg exists: f(a1)=f(a2)f(a_1) = f(a_2)f(a1​)=f(a2​) gives a1=g(f(a1))=g(f(a2))=a2a_1 = g(f(a_1)) = g(f(a_2)) = a_2a1​=g(f(a1​))=g(f(a2​))=a2​, so fff is injective; and any bbb equals f(g(b))f(g(b))f(g(b)), so fff is surjective. Conversely, if fff is bijective, each bbb has exactly one preimage; define g(b)g(b)g(b) to be it. Then both compositions are identities. ■\blacksquare■

Proposition 2.2 (pigeonhole). If AAA is a finite set and f:A→Af : A \to Af:A→A is injective, then fff is bijective.

Proof. An injective fff sends the ∣A∣\lvert A\rvert∣A∣ elements of AAA to ∣A∣\lvert A\rvert∣A∣ distinct elements of AAA, so the image is all of AAA. ■\blacksquare■

This small fact drives the proofs of Fermat's little theorem below and of Cayley's theorem later in the series. It is false for infinite sets: x↦2xx \mapsto 2xx↦2x on Z\mathbb{Z}Z is injective but not surjective.

Equivalence relations

A relation ∼\sim∼ on AAA is an equivalence relation if it is

  • reflexive: a∼aa \sim aa∼a for all aaa;
  • symmetric: a∼ba \sim ba∼b implies b∼ab \sim ab∼a;
  • transitive: a∼ba \sim ba∼b and b∼cb \sim cb∼c imply a∼ca \sim ca∼c.

The equivalence class of aaa is [a]={x∈A:x∼a}[a] = \{x \in A : x \sim a\}[a]={x∈A:x∼a}.

Examples: equality on any set; "same birthday" on people; "a−ba - ba−b is divisible by nnn" on Z\mathbb{Z}Z (Chapter 5); "same determinant" on 2×22 \times 22×2 matrices. Non-examples: ≤\leq≤ on R\mathbb{R}R is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric; "∣a−b∣≤1\lvert a - b\rvert \leq 1∣a−b∣≤1" on R\mathbb{R}R is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive (0∼10 \sim 10∼1, 1∼21 \sim 21∼2, but 0≁20 \not\sim 20∼2).

A partition of AAA is a collection of non-empty subsets of AAA such that every element of AAA lies in exactly one of them.

Theorem 2.3 (equivalence relations = partitions). If ∼\sim∼ is an equivalence relation on AAA, its equivalence classes form a partition of AAA. Conversely, every partition P\mathcal{P}P of AAA comes from exactly one equivalence relation: a∼ba \sim ba∼b if and only if aaa and bbb lie in the same block of P\mathcal{P}P.

Proof. Each class is non-empty and every aaa lies in a class, because a∈[a]a \in [a]a∈[a] by reflexivity. It remains to show that two classes are either equal or disjoint. Suppose c∈[a]∩[b]c \in [a] \cap [b]c∈[a]∩[b], so c∼ac \sim ac∼a and c∼bc \sim bc∼b. Take any x∈[a]x \in [a]x∈[a]: then x∼ax \sim ax∼a, a∼ca \sim ca∼c (symmetry), c∼bc \sim bc∼b, so x∼bx \sim bx∼b by transitivity twice, and x∈[b]x \in [b]x∈[b]. Hence [a]⊆[b][a] \subseteq [b][a]⊆[b], and by the same argument [b]⊆[a][b] \subseteq [a][b]⊆[a]. So overlapping classes are equal.

Conversely, given a partition, "same block" is reflexive (every element is in a block), symmetric (obvious), and transitive (if a,ba, ba,b share block PPP and b,cb, cb,c share block QQQ, then b∈P∩Qb \in P \cap Qb∈P∩Q, so P=QP = QP=Q because blocks are disjoint). Its classes are exactly the blocks. ■\blacksquare■

Trick: to show two classes are equal it is enough to find one common element. This "one overlap means equal" step is used again for cosets in post 02, where it gives Lagrange's theorem almost for free.

Chapter 3 — Divisibility, gcd and the Euclidean algorithm

Terminology

  • aaa divides bbb, written a∣ba \mid ba∣b, if b=akb = akb=ak for some integer kkk. Every integer divides 000; 000 divides only 000.
  • A prime is an integer p≥2p \geq 2p≥2 whose only positive divisors are 111 and ppp. An integer n≥2n \geq 2n≥2 that is not prime is composite.
  • The greatest common divisor gcd⁡(a,b)\gcd(a, b)gcd(a,b) of integers not both zero is the largest integer dividing both. Set gcd⁡(0,0)=0\gcd(0, 0) = 0gcd(0,0)=0.
  • aaa and bbb are coprime (relatively prime) if gcd⁡(a,b)=1\gcd(a, b) = 1gcd(a,b)=1.
  • Well-ordering principle: every non-empty set of non-negative integers has a least element. It is equivalent to induction and is taken as an axiom about N\mathbb{N}N.

The division algorithm

Theorem 3.1 (division algorithm). For integers aaa and bbb with b>0b > 0b>0 there are unique integers q,rq, rq,r with

a=qb+r,0≤r<b.a = qb + r, \qquad 0 \leq r < b. a=qb+r,0≤r<b.

Proof. Existence: let S={a−kb:k∈Z, a−kb≥0}S = \{a - kb : k \in \mathbb{Z}, \ a - kb \geq 0\}S={a−kb:k∈Z, a−kb≥0}. SSS is non-empty (take k=−∣a∣k = -\lvert a\rvertk=−∣a∣; then a−kb=a+∣a∣b≥a+∣a∣≥0a - kb = a + \lvert a\rvert b \geq a + \lvert a\rvert \geq 0a−kb=a+∣a∣b≥a+∣a∣≥0). By well-ordering SSS has a least element r=a−qb≥0r = a - qb \geq 0r=a−qb≥0. If r≥br \geq br≥b, then r−b=a−(q+1)br - b = a - (q+1)br−b=a−(q+1)b is a smaller element of SSS, a contradiction. So 0≤r<b0 \leq r < b0≤r<b.

Uniqueness: if qb+r=q′b+r′qb + r = q'b + r'qb+r=q′b+r′ with both remainders in [0,b)[0, b)[0,b), then b(q−q′)=r′−rb(q - q') = r' - rb(q−q′)=r′−r and ∣r′−r∣<b\lvert r' - r\rvert < b∣r′−r∣<b. The only multiple of bbb strictly between −b-b−b and bbb is 000, so r=r′r = r'r=r′ and q=q′q = q'q=q′. ■\blacksquare■

For negative aaa the remainder is still non-negative: −17=(−4)⋅5+3-17 = (-4) \cdot 5 + 3−17=(−4)⋅5+3, not (−3)⋅5−2(-3) \cdot 5 - 2(−3)⋅5−2.

Common pitfall: in many programming languages -17 % 5 returns -2 (C, Java, JavaScript) while Python returns 3. Mathematics always uses 0≤r<b0 \leq r < b0≤r<b.

The Euclidean algorithm

Lemma 3.2. If a=qb+ra = qb + ra=qb+r, then gcd⁡(a,b)=gcd⁡(b,r)\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, r)gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,r).

Proof. Any common divisor of aaa and bbb divides r=a−qbr = a - qbr=a−qb; any common divisor of bbb and rrr divides a=qb+ra = qb + ra=qb+r. The two pairs have the same common divisors, so the same greatest one. ■\blacksquare■

Repeating the division algorithm, the remainders strictly decrease and so reach 000; the last non-zero remainder is the gcd. For gcd⁡(240,46)\gcd(240, 46)gcd(240,46):

240=5⋅46+1046=4⋅10+610=1⋅6+46=1⋅4+24=2⋅2+0\begin{aligned} 240 &= 5 \cdot 46 + 10 \\ 46 &= 4 \cdot 10 + 6 \\ 10 &= 1 \cdot 6 + 4 \\ 6 &= 1 \cdot 4 + 2 \\ 4 &= 2 \cdot 2 + 0 \end{aligned} 240461064​=5⋅46+10=4⋅10+6=1⋅6+4=1⋅4+2=2⋅2+0​

So gcd⁡(240,46)=2\gcd(240, 46) = 2gcd(240,46)=2. The number of steps is small: it grows like the number of digits (Lamé's theorem bounds it by five times the number of decimal digits of the smaller number).

Bézout's identity and the extended algorithm

Theorem 3.3 (Bézout). For integers a,ba, ba,b not both zero, there are integers x,yx, yx,y with ax+by=gcd⁡(a,b)ax + by = \gcd(a, b)ax+by=gcd(a,b). Moreover gcd⁡(a,b)\gcd(a, b)gcd(a,b) is the smallest positive integer of the form ax+byax + byax+by.

Proof. Let S={ax+by:x,y∈Z}∩{1,2,3,… }S = \{ax + by : x, y \in \mathbb{Z}\} \cap \{1, 2, 3, \dots\}S={ax+by:x,y∈Z}∩{1,2,3,…}. It is non-empty (it contains a2+b2>0a^2 + b^2 > 0a2+b2>0), so it has a least element d=ax0+by0d = ax_0 + by_0d=ax0​+by0​. Divide: a=qd+ra = qd + ra=qd+r with 0≤r<d0 \leq r < d0≤r<d. Then r=a−q(ax0+by0)=a(1−qx0)+b(−qy0)r = a - q(ax_0 + by_0) = a(1 - qx_0) + b(-qy_0)r=a−q(ax0​+by0​)=a(1−qx0​)+b(−qy0​) has the same form, so by minimality r=0r = 0r=0 and d∣ad \mid ad∣a. Likewise d∣bd \mid bd∣b. Any common divisor ccc of a,ba, ba,b divides ax0+by0=dax_0 + by_0 = dax0​+by0​=d, so c≤dc \leq dc≤d. Hence d=gcd⁡(a,b)d = \gcd(a, b)d=gcd(a,b). ■\blacksquare■

The proof shows x,yx, yx,y exist but does not find them. The extended Euclidean algorithm does: keep, next to every remainder rir_iri​, integers si,tis_i, t_isi​,ti​ with ri=240si+46tir_i = 240 s_i + 46 t_iri​=240si​+46ti​. Start with r0=240=240⋅1+46⋅0r_0 = 240 = 240 \cdot 1 + 46 \cdot 0r0​=240=240⋅1+46⋅0 and r1=46=240⋅0+46⋅1r_1 = 46 = 240 \cdot 0 + 46 \cdot 1r1​=46=240⋅0+46⋅1; each new row is "row two above minus qqq times row above".

Euclid's lemma

Theorem 3.4 (Euclid's lemma). If a∣bca \mid bca∣bc and gcd⁡(a,b)=1\gcd(a, b) = 1gcd(a,b)=1, then a∣ca \mid ca∣c. In particular, if a prime ppp divides bcbcbc, then p∣bp \mid bp∣b or p∣cp \mid cp∣c.

Proof. By Bézout, ax+by=1ax + by = 1ax+by=1 for some x,yx, yx,y. Multiply by ccc: c=acx+bcyc = acx + bcyc=acx+bcy. The number aaa divides acxacxacx and divides bcybcybcy (because a∣bca \mid bca∣bc), so a∣ca \mid ca∣c. For the prime case: if p∤bp \nmid bp∤b then gcd⁡(p,b)=1\gcd(p, b) = 1gcd(p,b)=1 (the only positive divisors of ppp are 111 and ppp), so p∣cp \mid cp∣c. ■\blacksquare■

Watch out: the prime hypothesis matters. 6∣4⋅9=366 \mid 4 \cdot 9 = 366∣4⋅9=36 but 6∤46 \nmid 46∤4 and 6∤96 \nmid 96∤9.

Chapter 4 — The fundamental theorem of arithmetic

Theorem 4.1 (fundamental theorem of arithmetic). Every integer n≥2n \geq 2n≥2 can be written as a product of primes n=p1p2⋯pkn = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_kn=p1​p2​⋯pk​, and this factorisation is unique up to the order of the factors.

Proof. Existence, by strong induction on nnn. If nnn is prime, it is its own factorisation. Otherwise n=abn = abn=ab with 2≤a,b<n2 \leq a, b < n2≤a,b<n; by the induction hypothesis both aaa and bbb are products of primes, so nnn is too.

Uniqueness, by induction on nnn. Suppose n=p1⋯pk=q1⋯qln = p_1 \cdots p_k = q_1 \cdots q_ln=p1​⋯pk​=q1​⋯ql​ with all pi,qjp_i, q_jpi​,qj​ prime. Then p1p_1p1​ divides q1⋯qlq_1 \cdots q_lq1​⋯ql​, so by Euclid's lemma (applied repeatedly) p1∣qjp_1 \mid q_jp1​∣qj​ for some jjj. Since qjq_jqj​ is prime and p1≥2p_1 \geq 2p1​≥2, p1=qjp_1 = q_jp1​=qj​. Reorder so that j=1j = 1j=1 and cancel: p2⋯pk=q2⋯qlp_2 \cdots p_k = q_2 \cdots q_lp2​⋯pk​=q2​⋯ql​ is a smaller number (or both sides are empty products equal to 111), and by induction the remaining primes agree up to order. ■\blacksquare■

Grouping equal primes gives the canonical form n=p1e1⋯prern = p_1^{e_1} \cdots p_r^{e_r}n=p1e1​​⋯prer​​ with p1<⋯<prp_1 < \dots < p_rp1​<⋯<pr​. Examples: 360=23⋅32⋅5360 = 2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5360=23⋅32⋅5, 1001=7⋅11⋅131001 = 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 131001=7⋅11⋅13, 2026=2⋅10132026 = 2 \cdot 10132026=2⋅1013.

Corollary 4.2 (Euclid). There are infinitely many primes.

Proof. Given primes p1,…,pkp_1, \dots, p_kp1​,…,pk​, the number N=p1⋯pk+1N = p_1 \cdots p_k + 1N=p1​⋯pk​+1 has a prime factor ppp by Theorem 4.1. If ppp were some pip_ipi​, then ppp would divide N−p1⋯pk=1N - p_1 \cdots p_k = 1N−p1​⋯pk​=1, which is impossible. So no finite list contains every prime. ■\blacksquare■

Uniqueness is not automatic. In the set {a+b−5:a,b∈Z}\{a + b\sqrt{-5} : a, b \in \mathbb{Z}\}{a+b−5​:a,b∈Z}, 6=2⋅3=(1+−5)(1−−5)6 = 2 \cdot 3 = (1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5})6=2⋅3=(1+−5​)(1−−5​) gives two genuinely different factorisations into elements that cannot be split further. Explaining when unique factorisation holds is one of the main themes of ring theory (post 04).

Chapter 5 — Congruences and Z/nZ\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}Z/nZ

Terminology

  • Fix an integer n≥1n \geq 1n≥1, the modulus. aaa is congruent to bbb modulo nnn, written a≡b(modn)a \equiv b \pmod{n}a≡b(modn), if n∣a−bn \mid a - bn∣a−b.
  • The class of aaa is [a]n={a+kn:k∈Z}[a]_n = \{a + kn : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}[a]n​={a+kn:k∈Z}, also written aˉ\bar{a}aˉ or just aaa when the modulus is clear.
  • Z/nZ\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}Z/nZ (also written Zn\mathbb{Z}_nZn​) is the set of the nnn classes [0],[1],…,[n−1][0], [1], \dots, [n-1][0],[1],…,[n−1].
  • A class [a][a][a] is a unit if there is [b][b][b] with [a][b]=[1][a][b] = [1][a][b]=[1]. The units form (Z/nZ)×(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times(Z/nZ)×, also written U(n)U(n)U(n).
  • A non-zero class [a][a][a] is a zero divisor if [a][b]=[0][a][b] = [0][a][b]=[0] for some non-zero [b][b][b].

Congruence mod nnn is an equivalence relation: n∣0n \mid 0n∣0 (reflexive); n∣a−bn \mid a - bn∣a−b implies n∣b−an \mid b - an∣b−a (symmetric); n∣a−bn \mid a - bn∣a−b and n∣b−cn \mid b - cn∣b−c imply n∣a−cn \mid a - cn∣a−c (transitive). By Theorem 2.3 its classes partition Z\mathbb{Z}Z, and by the division algorithm each class contains exactly one of 0,1,…,n−10, 1, \dots, n-10,1,…,n−1, so there are exactly nnn classes.

Arithmetic on classes

Define [a]+[b]=[a+b][a] + [b] = [a + b][a]+[b]=[a+b] and [a]⋅[b]=[ab][a] \cdot [b] = [ab][a]⋅[b]=[ab].

Proposition 5.1. These operations are well defined: the result does not depend on which representatives are chosen.

Proof. Suppose a≡a′a \equiv a'a≡a′ and b≡b′b \equiv b'b≡b′, say a′=a+kna' = a + kna′=a+kn and b′=b+lnb' = b + lnb′=b+ln. Then a′+b′=a+b+(k+l)n≡a+ba' + b' = a + b + (k + l)n \equiv a + ba′+b′=a+b+(k+l)n≡a+b and a′b′=ab+(al+bk+kln)n≡aba'b' = ab + (al + bk + kln)n \equiv aba′b′=ab+(al+bk+kln)n≡ab. ■\blacksquare■

"Well defined" is the central worry whenever an operation is defined on classes through representatives. The same check, done for cosets, is what forces the definition of a normal subgroup in post 02.

In practice: reduce early and often. For example 3100 mod 73^{100} \bmod 73100mod7: 36≡1(mod7)3^6 \equiv 1 \pmod 736≡1(mod7) (checked below), and 100=6⋅16+4100 = 6 \cdot 16 + 4100=6⋅16+4, so 3100=(36)16⋅34≡34=81≡4(mod7)3^{100} = (3^6)^{16} \cdot 3^4 \equiv 3^4 = 81 \equiv 4 \pmod 73100=(36)16⋅34≡34=81≡4(mod7).

Units and zero divisors

In Z/12Z\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}Z/12Z: [3][4]=[12]=[0][3][4] = [12] = [0][3][4]=[12]=[0], so [3][3][3] and [4][4][4] are zero divisors. On the other hand [5][5]=[25]=[1][5][5] = [25] = [1][5][5]=[25]=[1], [7][7]=[49]=[1][7][7] = [49] = [1][7][7]=[49]=[1] and [11][11]=[121]=[1][11][11] = [121] = [1][11][11]=[121]=[1]. The units are exactly [1],[5],[7],[11][1], [5], [7], [11][1],[5],[7],[11], the classes coprime to 121212, and each of them is its own inverse.

Theorem 5.2. [a][a][a] is a unit in Z/nZ\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}Z/nZ if and only if gcd⁡(a,n)=1\gcd(a, n) = 1gcd(a,n)=1. If gcd⁡(a,n)=d>1\gcd(a, n) = d > 1gcd(a,n)=d>1 and n∤an \nmid an∤a, then [a][a][a] is a zero divisor.

Proof. If gcd⁡(a,n)=1\gcd(a, n) = 1gcd(a,n)=1, Bézout gives ax+ny=1ax + ny = 1ax+ny=1, so ax≡1ax \equiv 1ax≡1 and [x][x][x] is the inverse. Conversely if ab≡1ab \equiv 1ab≡1, then ab−1=knab - 1 = knab−1=kn, so ab−kn=1ab - kn = 1ab−kn=1 and every common divisor of aaa and nnn divides 111. For the last claim: a⋅(n/d)=(a/d)⋅n≡0a \cdot (n/d) = (a/d) \cdot n \equiv 0a⋅(n/d)=(a/d)⋅n≡0, and [n/d]≠[0][n/d] \neq [0][n/d]=[0] because 0<n/d<n0 < n/d < n0<n/d<n. ■\blacksquare■

Corollary 5.3. Z/nZ\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}Z/nZ has every non-zero class invertible if and only if nnn is prime.

Theorem 5.2 is also an algorithm: the inverse is the Bézout coefficient. To invert 171717 modulo 434343: 43=2⋅17+943 = 2 \cdot 17 + 943=2⋅17+9, 17=1⋅9+817 = 1 \cdot 9 + 817=1⋅9+8, 9=1⋅8+19 = 1 \cdot 8 + 19=1⋅8+1. Back-substitute: 1=9−8=9−(17−9)=2⋅9−17=2(43−2⋅17)−17=2⋅43−5⋅171 = 9 - 8 = 9 - (17 - 9) = 2 \cdot 9 - 17 = 2(43 - 2 \cdot 17) - 17 = 2 \cdot 43 - 5 \cdot 171=9−8=9−(17−9)=2⋅9−17=2(43−2⋅17)−17=2⋅43−5⋅17. So 17−1≡−5≡38(mod43)17^{-1} \equiv -5 \equiv 38 \pmod{43}17−1≡−5≡38(mod43). Check: 17⋅38=646=15⋅43+117 \cdot 38 = 646 = 15 \cdot 43 + 117⋅38=646=15⋅43+1.

Linear congruences

Theorem 5.4. The congruence ax≡b(modn)ax \equiv b \pmod nax≡b(modn) has a solution if and only if d=gcd⁡(a,n)d = \gcd(a, n)d=gcd(a,n) divides bbb. In that case it has exactly ddd solutions modulo nnn.

Proof sketch. A solution means ax−ny=bax - ny = bax−ny=b for some yyy, and by Bézout the values of ax−nyax - nyax−ny are exactly the multiples of ddd. If d∣bd \mid bd∣b, divide through: (a/d)x≡b/d(modn/d)(a/d)x \equiv b/d \pmod{n/d}(a/d)x≡b/d(modn/d), and a/da/da/d is a unit mod n/dn/dn/d, so xxx is unique mod n/dn/dn/d. That single class mod n/dn/dn/d splits into ddd classes mod nnn. ■\blacksquare■

Example: 14x≡6(mod20)14x \equiv 6 \pmod{20}14x≡6(mod20). Here gcd⁡(14,20)=2\gcd(14, 20) = 2gcd(14,20)=2 divides 666. Divide by 2: 7x≡3(mod10)7x \equiv 3 \pmod{10}7x≡3(mod10). Since 7⋅3=21≡17 \cdot 3 = 21 \equiv 17⋅3=21≡1, 7−1≡3(mod10)7^{-1} \equiv 3 \pmod{10}7−1≡3(mod10), so x≡9(mod10)x \equiv 9 \pmod{10}x≡9(mod10), giving x≡9x \equiv 9x≡9 or 19(mod20)19 \pmod{20}19(mod20). Check: 14⋅9=126=6⋅20+614 \cdot 9 = 126 = 6 \cdot 20 + 614⋅9=126=6⋅20+6 and 14⋅19=266=13⋅20+614 \cdot 19 = 266 = 13 \cdot 20 + 614⋅19=266=13⋅20+6.

Common pitfall: you may not "divide both sides" of a congruence by a number that is not a unit. 2⋅3≡2⋅9(mod12)2 \cdot 3 \equiv 2 \cdot 9 \pmod{12}2⋅3≡2⋅9(mod12), but 3≢9(mod12)3 \not\equiv 9 \pmod{12}3≡9(mod12). Division by aaa modulo nnn is multiplication by a−1a^{-1}a−1, which exists only when gcd⁡(a,n)=1\gcd(a, n) = 1gcd(a,n)=1; otherwise the modulus must be divided too, as above.

Chapter 6 — Euler's phi, Fermat and Euler

Euler's phi function

φ(n)\varphi(n)φ(n) is the number of integers in {1,…,n}\{1, \dots, n\}{1,…,n} coprime to nnn; by Theorem 5.2 it is the number of units, φ(n)=∣(Z/nZ)×∣\varphi(n) = \lvert(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times\rvertφ(n)=∣(Z/nZ)×∣.

  • For a prime ppp: φ(p)=p−1\varphi(p) = p - 1φ(p)=p−1.
  • For a prime power: φ(pk)=pk−pk−1\varphi(p^k) = p^k - p^{k-1}φ(pk)=pk−pk−1, because the numbers in {1,…,pk}\{1, \dots, p^k\}{1,…,pk} not coprime to pkp^kpk are exactly the pk−1p^{k-1}pk−1 multiples of ppp.
  • Multiplicative: if gcd⁡(m,n)=1\gcd(m, n) = 1gcd(m,n)=1 then φ(mn)=φ(m)φ(n)\varphi(mn) = \varphi(m)\varphi(n)φ(mn)=φ(m)φ(n). This follows from the Chinese remainder theorem (Chapter 7): aaa is coprime to mnmnmn exactly when it is coprime to both mmm and nnn, and the CRT bijection matches such aaa with pairs of units.

Together these give, for n=p1e1⋯prern = p_1^{e_1} \cdots p_r^{e_r}n=p1e1​​⋯prer​​,

φ(n)=n∏p∣n(1−1p).\varphi(n) = n \prod_{p \mid n} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p}\right). φ(n)=np∣n∏​(1−p1​).

Examples: φ(12)=12⋅12⋅23=4\varphi(12) = 12 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac23 = 4φ(12)=12⋅21​⋅32​=4 (the units 1,5,7,111, 5, 7, 111,5,7,11); φ(36)=36⋅12⋅23=12\varphi(36) = 36 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac23 = 12φ(36)=36⋅21​⋅32​=12; φ(100)=100⋅12⋅45=40\varphi(100) = 100 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac45 = 40φ(100)=100⋅21​⋅54​=40; φ(35)=φ(5)φ(7)=4⋅6=24\varphi(35) = \varphi(5)\varphi(7) = 4 \cdot 6 = 24φ(35)=φ(5)φ(7)=4⋅6=24.

Fermat's little theorem

Theorem 6.1 (Fermat's little theorem). If ppp is prime and p∤ap \nmid ap∤a, then ap−1≡1(modp)a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod pap−1≡1(modp). Consequently ap≡a(modp)a^p \equiv a \pmod pap≡a(modp) for every integer aaa.

Proof. Consider the map x↦axx \mapsto axx↦ax on the set R={[1],[2],…,[p−1]}R = \{[1], [2], \dots, [p-1]\}R={[1],[2],…,[p−1]} of non-zero classes mod ppp. It lands in RRR (a product of two units is a unit, so never [0][0][0]) and is injective, because ax≡ayax \equiv ayax≡ay implies x≡yx \equiv yx≡y after multiplying by a−1a^{-1}a−1. By the pigeonhole Proposition 2.2 it is a bijection, so it just reorders RRR. Multiply all elements of RRR both ways:

(a⋅1)(a⋅2)⋯(a⋅(p−1))≡1⋅2⋯(p−1)(modp),(a \cdot 1)(a \cdot 2) \cdots (a \cdot (p-1)) \equiv 1 \cdot 2 \cdots (p-1) \pmod p, (a⋅1)(a⋅2)⋯(a⋅(p−1))≡1⋅2⋯(p−1)(modp),

that is ap−1(p−1)!≡(p−1)!(modp)a^{p-1} (p-1)! \equiv (p-1)! \pmod pap−1(p−1)!≡(p−1)!(modp). Every factor of (p−1)!(p-1)!(p−1)! is a unit, so (p−1)!(p-1)!(p−1)! is a unit and can be cancelled: ap−1≡1a^{p-1} \equiv 1ap−1≡1. For the second statement multiply by aaa; if p∣ap \mid ap∣a both sides are 000. ■\blacksquare■

Check with p=7p = 7p=7, a=3a = 3a=3: multiplying 1,2,3,4,5,61, 2, 3, 4, 5, 61,2,3,4,5,6 by 3 gives 3,6,2,5,1,43, 6, 2, 5, 1, 43,6,2,5,1,4 modulo 7, the same six classes in a new order, and 36=729=104⋅7+13^6 = 729 = 104 \cdot 7 + 136=729=104⋅7+1.

Euler's theorem

Theorem 6.2 (Euler). If gcd⁡(a,n)=1\gcd(a, n) = 1gcd(a,n)=1, then aφ(n)≡1(modn)a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod naφ(n)≡1(modn).

Proof. Repeat the proof above with the set UUU of the φ(n)\varphi(n)φ(n) units mod nnn instead of RRR: x↦axx \mapsto axx↦ax permutes UUU, so aφ(n)∏u∈Uu≡∏u∈Uua^{\varphi(n)} \prod_{u \in U} u \equiv \prod_{u \in U} uaφ(n)∏u∈U​u≡∏u∈U​u, and the product of units is a unit, so it cancels. ■\blacksquare■

Fermat is the case n=pn = pn=p. Post 02 re-proves both in one line from Lagrange's theorem, because (Z/nZ)×(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times(Z/nZ)× is a group of order φ(n)\varphi(n)φ(n) and the order of an element divides the order of the group.

Example: the last digit of 72227^{222}7222. φ(10)=4\varphi(10) = 4φ(10)=4 and gcd⁡(7,10)=1\gcd(7, 10) = 1gcd(7,10)=1, so 74≡1(mod10)7^4 \equiv 1 \pmod{10}74≡1(mod10). Since 222=4⋅55+2222 = 4 \cdot 55 + 2222=4⋅55+2, 7222≡72=49≡97^{222} \equiv 7^2 = 49 \equiv 97222≡72=49≡9. The last digit is 9.

Watch out: Euler's theorem needs gcd⁡(a,n)=1\gcd(a, n) = 1gcd(a,n)=1. 2φ(4)=22=4≡0(mod4)2^{\varphi(4)} = 2^2 = 4 \equiv 0 \pmod 42φ(4)=22=4≡0(mod4), not 1. Also, φ(n)\varphi(n)φ(n) is an exponent that always works, not always the smallest one: modulo 12, every unit already satisfies u2≡1u^2 \equiv 1u2≡1 although φ(12)=4\varphi(12) = 4φ(12)=4.

Chapter 7 — The Chinese remainder theorem

Theorem 7.1 (Chinese remainder theorem). Let n1,…,nkn_1, \dots, n_kn1​,…,nk​ be pairwise coprime positive integers and N=n1⋯nkN = n_1 \cdots n_kN=n1​⋯nk​. For any integers a1,…,aka_1, \dots, a_ka1​,…,ak​ the system

x≡a1(modn1),…,x≡ak(modnk)x \equiv a_1 \pmod{n_1}, \quad \dots, \quad x \equiv a_k \pmod{n_k} x≡a1​(modn1​),…,x≡ak​(modnk​)

has a solution, and any two solutions are congruent modulo NNN.

Proof. Existence: put Ni=N/niN_i = N / n_iNi​=N/ni​. Since nin_ini​ is coprime to every other njn_jnj​, it is coprime to NiN_iNi​, so there is MiM_iMi​ with NiMi≡1(modni)N_i M_i \equiv 1 \pmod{n_i}Ni​Mi​≡1(modni​). Let x=∑iaiNiMix = \sum_i a_i N_i M_ix=∑i​ai​Ni​Mi​. Modulo njn_jnj​, every term with i≠ji \neq ji=j vanishes (because nj∣Nin_j \mid N_inj​∣Ni​), and the jjj-th term is aj⋅1a_j \cdot 1aj​⋅1. Uniqueness: if x,x′x, x'x,x′ both work, each nin_ini​ divides x−x′x - x'x−x′; the nin_ini​ are pairwise coprime, so (by Euclid's lemma, repeatedly) their product NNN divides x−x′x - x'x−x′. ■\blacksquare■

Worked example (Sunzi's classic puzzle). Find xxx with x≡2(mod3)x \equiv 2 \pmod 3x≡2(mod3), x≡3(mod5)x \equiv 3 \pmod 5x≡3(mod5), x≡2(mod7)x \equiv 2 \pmod 7x≡2(mod7). Here N=105N = 105N=105.

iii nin_ini​ aia_iai​ Ni=N/niN_i = N/n_iNi​=N/ni​ Ni mod niN_i \bmod n_iNi​modni​ MiM_iMi​ aiNiMia_i N_i M_iai​Ni​Mi​
1 3 2 35 2 2 140
2 5 3 21 1 1 63
3 7 2 15 1 1 30

Sum: 140+63+30=233≡23(mod105)140 + 63 + 30 = 233 \equiv 23 \pmod{105}140+63+30=233≡23(mod105). Check: 23=7⋅3+223 = 7 \cdot 3 + 223=7⋅3+2, 23=4⋅5+323 = 4 \cdot 5 + 323=4⋅5+3, 23=3⋅7+223 = 3 \cdot 7 + 223=3⋅7+2.

In structural language, the theorem says that the map Z/NZ→Z/n1Z×⋯×Z/nkZ\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/n_1\mathbb{Z} \times \dots \times \mathbb{Z}/n_k\mathbb{Z}Z/NZ→Z/n1​Z×⋯×Z/nk​Z, [x]↦([x]n1,…,[x]nk)[x] \mapsto ([x]_{n_1}, \dots, [x]_{n_k})[x]↦([x]n1​​,…,[x]nk​​), is a bijection that respects addition and multiplication. Both sides have NNN elements, so it is enough to know the map is injective, which is the uniqueness part. Post 01 meets the additive version as "Z/6Z\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}Z/6Z is the same group as Z/2Z×Z/3Z\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}Z/2Z×Z/3Z", and post 04 the ring version.

Common pitfall: the moduli must be pairwise coprime. The system x≡0(mod4)x \equiv 0 \pmod 4x≡0(mod4), x≡1(mod6)x \equiv 1 \pmod 6x≡1(mod6) has no solution: the first says xxx is even, the second says xxx is odd.

Chapter 8 — A toy RSA

RSA (Rivest, Shamir and Adleman, 1978) is Euler's theorem put to work. The numbers below are tiny so that every step can be checked by hand; real keys use primes of about 1024 bits or more and a padding scheme, and textbook RSA as shown here is not secure.

Key generation.

  1. Pick primes p=11p = 11p=11, q=17q = 17q=17. The modulus is n=pq=187n = pq = 187n=pq=187.
  2. φ(n)=(p−1)(q−1)=10⋅16=160\varphi(n) = (p-1)(q-1) = 10 \cdot 16 = 160φ(n)=(p−1)(q−1)=10⋅16=160.
  3. Pick a public exponent eee coprime to 160: e=7e = 7e=7.
  4. The private exponent is d=e−1 mod φ(n)d = e^{-1} \bmod \varphi(n)d=e−1modφ(n): since 7⋅23=161=160+17 \cdot 23 = 161 = 160 + 17⋅23=161=160+1, d=23d = 23d=23.

Public key (n,e)=(187,7)(n, e) = (187, 7)(n,e)=(187,7); private key d=23d = 23d=23.

Encryption of the message m=88m = 88m=88 (any integer with 0≤m<n0 \leq m < n0≤m<n): c=me mod nc = m^e \bmod nc=memodn, computed by repeated squaring so that no number exceeds 1862186^21862:

882=7744≡77(mod187)884≡772=5929≡132887=884⋅882⋅88≡132⋅77⋅88≡66⋅88=5808≡11\begin{aligned} 88^2 &= 7744 \equiv 77 \pmod{187} \\ 88^4 &\equiv 77^2 = 5929 \equiv 132 \\ 88^7 &= 88^4 \cdot 88^2 \cdot 88 \equiv 132 \cdot 77 \cdot 88 \equiv 66 \cdot 88 = 5808 \equiv 11 \end{aligned} 882884887​=7744≡77(mod187)≡772=5929≡132=884⋅882⋅88≡132⋅77⋅88≡66⋅88=5808≡11​

So the ciphertext is c=11c = 11c=11.

Decryption: cd=1123 mod 187c^d = 11^{23} \bmod 187cd=1123mod187. Write 23=16+4+2+123 = 16 + 4 + 2 + 123=16+4+2+1 and square repeatedly: 112=12111^2 = 121112=121, 114≡1212=14641≡5511^4 \equiv 121^2 = 14641 \equiv 55114≡1212=14641≡55, 118≡552=3025≡3311^8 \equiv 55^2 = 3025 \equiv 33118≡552=3025≡33, 1116≡332=1089≡15411^{16} \equiv 33^2 = 1089 \equiv 1541116≡332=1089≡154. Then

1123≡154⋅55⋅121⋅11≡55⋅121⋅11≡110⋅11=1210≡88(mod187).11^{23} \equiv 154 \cdot 55 \cdot 121 \cdot 11 \equiv 55 \cdot 121 \cdot 11 \equiv 110 \cdot 11 = 1210 \equiv 88 \pmod{187}. 1123≡154⋅55⋅121⋅11≡55⋅121⋅11≡110⋅11=1210≡88(mod187).

The original message comes back.

Why it works. ed=1+kφ(n)ed = 1 + k\varphi(n)ed=1+kφ(n) for some k≥0k \geq 0k≥0. If gcd⁡(m,n)=1\gcd(m, n) = 1gcd(m,n)=1, Euler gives med=m⋅(mφ(n))k≡m(modn)m^{ed} = m \cdot (m^{\varphi(n)})^k \equiv m \pmod nmed=m⋅(mφ(n))k≡m(modn). (If mmm shares a factor with nnn, the result still holds: check it modulo ppp and modulo qqq separately with Fermat, then combine with the CRT.)

Why it is believed hard to break. Anyone who knows φ(n)\varphi(n)φ(n) can compute ddd with the extended Euclidean algorithm, and φ(n)\varphi(n)φ(n) is easy from ppp and qqq. So the security rests on the difficulty of factoring nnn; no fast classical factoring algorithm is known.

Practice Exercises

1. Prove by induction that 6∣n3−n6 \mid n^3 - n6∣n3−n for every integer n≥0n \geq 0n≥0.

Solution

Base: 03−0=00^3 - 0 = 003−0=0. Step: (k+1)3−(k+1)=(k3−k)+3k2+3k=(k3−k)+3k(k+1)(k+1)^3 - (k+1) = (k^3 - k) + 3k^2 + 3k = (k^3 - k) + 3k(k+1)(k+1)3−(k+1)=(k3−k)+3k2+3k=(k3−k)+3k(k+1). The first term is divisible by 6 by hypothesis; k(k+1)k(k+1)k(k+1) is a product of consecutive integers, hence even, so 3k(k+1)3k(k+1)3k(k+1) is divisible by 6. (A direct proof also works: n3−n=(n−1)n(n+1)n^3 - n = (n-1)n(n+1)n3−n=(n−1)n(n+1) is a product of three consecutive integers, so it is divisible by 2 and by 3.)

2. On R2\mathbb{R}^2R2 define (x1,y1)∼(x2,y2)(x_1, y_1) \sim (x_2, y_2)(x1​,y1​)∼(x2​,y2​) if x12+y12=x22+y22x_1^2 + y_1^2 = x_2^2 + y_2^2x12​+y12​=x22​+y22​. Show this is an equivalence relation and describe the partition.

Solution

It is "f(p1)=f(p2)f(p_1) = f(p_2)f(p1​)=f(p2​)" for the function f(x,y)=x2+y2f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2f(x,y)=x2+y2, and any relation of that form inherits reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity from equality. The classes are the circles centred at the origin, plus the single point (0,0)(0,0)(0,0).

3. Use the extended Euclidean algorithm to find gcd⁡(252,198)\gcd(252, 198)gcd(252,198) and integers x,yx, yx,y with 252x+198y=gcd⁡(252,198)252x + 198y = \gcd(252, 198)252x+198y=gcd(252,198).

Solution

252=1⋅198+54252 = 1 \cdot 198 + 54252=1⋅198+54, 198=3⋅54+36198 = 3 \cdot 54 + 36198=3⋅54+36, 54=1⋅36+1854 = 1 \cdot 36 + 1854=1⋅36+18, 36=2⋅1836 = 2 \cdot 1836=2⋅18. So the gcd is 18. Back-substitute: 18=54−36=54−(198−3⋅54)=4⋅54−198=4(252−198)−198=4⋅252−5⋅19818 = 54 - 36 = 54 - (198 - 3 \cdot 54) = 4 \cdot 54 - 198 = 4(252 - 198) - 198 = 4 \cdot 252 - 5 \cdot 19818=54−36=54−(198−3⋅54)=4⋅54−198=4(252−198)−198=4⋅252−5⋅198. Check: 1008−990=181008 - 990 = 181008−990=18.

4. Find all solutions of 14x≡6(mod20)14x \equiv 6 \pmod{20}14x≡6(mod20) by the method of Theorem 5.4, and explain why 14x≡5(mod20)14x \equiv 5 \pmod{20}14x≡5(mod20) has none.

Solution

As in Chapter 5: x≡9x \equiv 9x≡9 or 19(mod20)19 \pmod{20}19(mod20). For the second congruence, gcd⁡(14,20)=2\gcd(14, 20) = 2gcd(14,20)=2 does not divide 5: the left side 14x−20y14x - 20y14x−20y is always even, the right side is odd.

5. Compute 21000 mod 132^{1000} \bmod 1321000mod13 and the last two digits of 320263^{2026}32026.

Solution

By Fermat 212≡1(mod13)2^{12} \equiv 1 \pmod{13}212≡1(mod13); 1000=12⋅83+41000 = 12 \cdot 83 + 41000=12⋅83+4, so 21000≡24=16≡32^{1000} \equiv 2^4 = 16 \equiv 321000≡24=16≡3. For the last two digits work mod 100: φ(100)=40\varphi(100) = 40φ(100)=40 and gcd⁡(3,100)=1\gcd(3, 100) = 1gcd(3,100)=1, so 340≡13^{40} \equiv 1340≡1; 2026=40⋅50+262026 = 40 \cdot 50 + 262026=40⋅50+26, so 32026≡3263^{2026} \equiv 3^{26}32026≡326. Now 35=243≡433^5 = 243 \equiv 4335=243≡43, 310≡432=1849≡493^{10} \equiv 43^2 = 1849 \equiv 49310≡432=1849≡49, 320≡492=2401≡13^{20} \equiv 49^2 = 2401 \equiv 1320≡492=2401≡1. (The order of 3 mod 100 is actually 20, a divisor of 40.) So 326≡36=729≡293^{26} \equiv 3^{6} = 729 \equiv 29326≡36=729≡29. The last two digits are 29.

6. Solve x≡3(mod4)x \equiv 3 \pmod 4x≡3(mod4), x≡4(mod9)x \equiv 4 \pmod 9x≡4(mod9).

Solution

N=36N = 36N=36. N1=9≡1(mod4)N_1 = 9 \equiv 1 \pmod 4N1​=9≡1(mod4), so M1=1M_1 = 1M1​=1; N2=4N_2 = 4N2​=4 and 4⋅7=28≡1(mod9)4 \cdot 7 = 28 \equiv 1 \pmod 94⋅7=28≡1(mod9), so M2=7M_2 = 7M2​=7. Then x=3⋅9⋅1+4⋅4⋅7=27+112=139≡31(mod36)x = 3 \cdot 9 \cdot 1 + 4 \cdot 4 \cdot 7 = 27 + 112 = 139 \equiv 31 \pmod{36}x=3⋅9⋅1+4⋅4⋅7=27+112=139≡31(mod36). Check: 31=7⋅4+331 = 7 \cdot 4 + 331=7⋅4+3 and 31=3⋅9+431 = 3 \cdot 9 + 431=3⋅9+4.

7. With p=5p = 5p=5, q=11q = 11q=11 and e=3e = 3e=3, find nnn, φ(n)\varphi(n)φ(n) and ddd; encrypt m=7m = 7m=7 and decrypt the result.

Solution

n=55n = 55n=55, φ(n)=4⋅10=40\varphi(n) = 4 \cdot 10 = 40φ(n)=4⋅10=40, d=27d = 27d=27 because 3⋅27=81=2⋅40+13 \cdot 27 = 81 = 2 \cdot 40 + 13⋅27=81=2⋅40+1. Encrypt: 73=343=6⋅55+137^3 = 343 = 6 \cdot 55 + 1373=343=6⋅55+13, so c=13c = 13c=13. Decrypt: 132=169≡413^2 = 169 \equiv 4132=169≡4, 134≡1613^4 \equiv 16134≡16, 138≡256≡3613^8 \equiv 256 \equiv 36138≡256≡36, 1316≡362=1296≡3113^{16} \equiv 36^2 = 1296 \equiv 311316≡362=1296≡31. With 27=16+8+2+127 = 16 + 8 + 2 + 127=16+8+2+1: 31⋅36=1116≡1631 \cdot 36 = 1116 \equiv 1631⋅36=1116≡16, 16⋅4=64≡916 \cdot 4 = 64 \equiv 916⋅4=64≡9, 9⋅13=117≡79 \cdot 13 = 117 \equiv 79⋅13=117≡7. The message 7 comes back.

Cheat-sheet

Idea Statement or method
Equivalence relation reflexive, symmetric, transitive; classes partition the set
Division algorithm a=qb+ra = qb + ra=qb+r, 0≤r<b0 \leq r < b0≤r<b, unique
Euclidean algorithm gcd⁡(a,b)=gcd⁡(b,a mod b)\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, a \bmod b)gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,amodb); last non-zero remainder
Bézout ax+by=gcd⁡(a,b)ax + by = \gcd(a, b)ax+by=gcd(a,b); gcd is the least positive such value
Extended Euclid new row = row two above minus qqq times row above
Euclid's lemma p∣bc⇒p∣bp \mid bc \Rightarrow p \mid bp∣bc⇒p∣b or p∣cp \mid cp∣c
FTA unique factorisation into primes, up to order
Z/nZ\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}Z/nZ nnn classes; +++ and ⋅\cdot⋅ well defined
Unit test [a][a][a] invertible iff gcd⁡(a,n)=1\gcd(a, n) = 1gcd(a,n)=1; inverse from Bézout
ax≡bax \equiv bax≡b solvable iff gcd⁡(a,n)∣b\gcd(a,n) \mid bgcd(a,n)∣b; then gcd⁡(a,n)\gcd(a,n)gcd(a,n) solutions
Euler phi φ(n)=n∏(1−1/p)\varphi(n) = n \prod (1 - 1/p)φ(n)=n∏(1−1/p) over primes p∣np \mid np∣n
Fermat ap−1≡1(modp)a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod pap−1≡1(modp) if p∤ap \nmid ap∤a
Euler aφ(n)≡1(modn)a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod naφ(n)≡1(modn) if gcd⁡(a,n)=1\gcd(a, n) = 1gcd(a,n)=1
CRT pairwise coprime moduli: unique solution mod N=∏niN = \prod n_iN=∏ni​
RSA n=pqn = pqn=pq, ed≡1(modφ(n))ed \equiv 1 \pmod{\varphi(n)}ed≡1(modφ(n)), c=mec = m^ec=me, m=cdm = c^dm=cd mod nnn

What's next

Post 01 takes the pattern seen here (a set, one operation, an identity, inverses) and turns it into the definition of a group. Z\mathbb{Z}Z under addition, Z/nZ\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}Z/nZ under addition and (Z/nZ)×(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times(Z/nZ)× under multiplication become the first examples, joined by permutations, symmetries of polygons, invertible matrices and the quaternions. The division algorithm reappears in the proof that every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic, and gcd⁡\gcdgcd returns in the formula n/gcd⁡(k,n)n / \gcd(k, n)n/gcd(k,n) for the order of kkk in Z/nZ\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}Z/nZ.
